query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled pre-oxidation treatment that forms a uniform, nanocrystalline oxide layer on the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating will enhance wear resistance and reduce plastic deformation during high-temperature sliding by providing a stable, load‐bearing tribo-layer.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating with its standard microstructure and composition produced for high-temperature applications.
generation.intervention: Apply a pre-oxidation treatment designed to create a controlled nanocrystalline oxide layer on the coating surface before exposure to high-temperature sliding conditions.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding tests conducted under controlled normal load and sliding speed conditions, in the regime of 600–900°C.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a uniform, nanocrystalline oxide layer (for example, a spinel or Cr-rich oxide) on the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: The pre-formed oxide layer is expected to act as a protective, lubricious barrier that minimizes direct metal–metal contact, thereby reducing adhesion and plastic deformation. This layer can absorb and redistribute frictional stresses during sliding, leading to lower wear rates and smoother deformation characteristics.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline as-deposited coating, the pre-oxidized coating will exhibit a lower specific wear rate, reduced friction coefficient, and less severe microscopic plastic deformation under high-temperature sliding conditions.
generation.baseline: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating in its as-deposited condition, without any pre-oxidation treatment.
generation.boundary: These predictions are expected to hold primarily under high-temperature sliding conditions (600–900°C) and may not apply at room temperature or under significantly different load or speed conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contributions of the oxide layer’s protective effects versus any concurrent grain refinement phenomena remain not fully quantified, and potential interactions with substrate properties could also influence the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coatings: one set receiving a controlled pre-oxidation treatment to develop the nanocrystalline oxide layer and a baseline set without such treatment. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature sliding tests (600–900°C) under controlled normal loads and sliding speeds.
measurements: Quantitative wear rate (volume loss per unit load and distance)
Microscopic analysis (SEM/EDS) of worn surfaces to assess the extent of oxide integrity and plastic deformation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the pre-oxidized coatings do not exhibit statistically significant improvements (e.g., lower wear rate and friction coefficient with reduced plastic deformation) compared to the baseline, or if any differences fall within experimental uncertainty.

frame.system: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate in its baseline microstructure and composition, as typically processed for high-temperature applications.
frame.goal: Identify and quantify the mechanistic role that microstructural evolution—specifically, the development of a stable nanocrystalline surface layer or protective oxide phase—plays in governing overall wear resistance and the microscopic deformation processes during sliding at elevated temperatures.
frame.limitation: There is an open question regarding which specific in situ physical changes (grain refinement, phase transformation, or oxide layer formation) under high-temperature sliding conditions predominantly dictate the wear resistance and deformation behavior of the coating.
constraints: must propose a single, testable mechanistic hypothesis
define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition
predict corresponding directional changes in wear and microscopic deformation
specify the high-temperature sliding regime where these predictions hold
specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis
frame.regime: High-temperature sliding regime (e.g., 600–900°C) under controlled normal load and sliding speeds representative of service conditions.
prior_attempts: Previous studies have explored the role of high-temperature oxidation and thermally induced grain boundary migration in similar alloy systems, but they have not isolated a single mechanistic factor or controlled variable that unifies wear resistance and deformation behavior.

Standard wear tests on bulk alloys and coatings have noted improvements with refined microstructures or protective oxide scales; however, these approaches did not experimentally decouple the contributions of microstructural evolution versus oxidation in the high-temperature sliding context.

decision.trend: Early studies (e.g., PMC5849017) established that mechanical processing of HEA coatings can lead to a nanocrystalline microstructure, which was later linked (PMC7311485) to improved wear and lower friction through inverse Hall-Petch effects. More recent work (PMC10908794) on similar HEA systems under high-temperature conditions showed that controlled thermal exposure can generate a protective oxide scale, contributing to enhanced wear resistance. The progression has been from understanding microstructural refinement effects at room temperature to exploring the role of in situ oxidation under service-like, elevated temperature conditions. However, the individual contributions of grain refinement (nanocrystalline surface layer) versus oxide phase formation to wear resistance and deformation under high-temperature sliding remain unclear.
decision.unsolved: It is still unresolved whether the dominant mechanism that governs wear resistance and microscopic deformation in high-temperature sliding for FeNiCrCoCu coatings is the formation of a stable, nanocrystalline surface layer or that of a protective oxide phase.
decision.lever: Implementing a pre-oxidation treatment to create a controlled, nanocrystalline oxide layer on the coating surface prior to sliding tests
decision.why: This experiment isolates the effect of oxide layer formation by comparing pre-oxidized coatings to the as-deposited baseline under identical high-temperature (600–900°C) sliding conditions. Given prior evidence that both nanocrystallization and oxidation can improve wear behavior, this controlled variable approach will directly test whether the presence of a pre-formed oxide layer is responsible for enhanced wear resistance and modified deformation behavior. A failure to observe the predicted deterioration in wear performance upon a reduction or removal of the oxide layer would falsify the hypothesis.
